coherence.reasons: Both documents run a consistent line from governing thought through sections to the board decisions, and both build the argument on the board's own constraints. X's governing thought carries the payback condition (hold ad cost near 28%), and its sections map cleanly onto five key questions. Y opens with a one-page card of every option against every board test, which makes the hierarchy explicit: A fails only the ambition, B fails three tests, J passes but builds no US business. Y also carries its unit-economics finding through to the recommendation: retail's $7.5M fixed cost needs about 4,200 doors, so the retail gate requires a self-funding retail case. X shows retail would need about 32 units per door a week to break even, but its retail gate (20% awareness, test doors, 4.0 units) never reconciles with that finding. X's 'demand is proven, and it is still climbing' also sits a little loosely against its own caveat that the payback threshold holds only if plan volumes do. Y has a trivial 28.5% versus 28.6% wobble.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: Amazon-led entry with gates, reject B, defer Japan, reset the $40M ambition, raise the awareness trigger to 20%. Y weighs the trade-offs more explicitly. It concedes the Head of Japan is right that J is safer and quantifies the choice: about $19M of 2030 revenue given up to avoid about $4M of cash downside. It names the risk the board accepts (payback not assured) and proposes a $4M cash envelope as a tripwire. Its guardrail is operational: ACoS at or below 28%, slow paid growth if above 30% for two quarters, and a re-plan to 27% or below if the tariff rises. It also sees that a full-cost national retail launch in 2029 would break payback even after the awareness gate, so it adds a self-funding retail gate and an ACoS condition on the $10M trigger. X's judgment is sound and includes a scorecard with 'if missed' actions, test doors and a 4.0 sell-through check. But X sets the ACoS threshold at exactly the 28.6% break-even with no margin or trigger action. Its Japan comparison rests mainly on revenue size, and it does not address how later retail fits within payback.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers accurately: $10.73 before ads, $4.73 / $4.01 / $3.05 by ACoS, retail about $7.55, B peak $20.8M, A at +2.4 / +0.4 / −2.3, break-even 28.6%, margin 4.5%, tariff case −0.7. Both test the 4.5 units and 25% ACoS assumptions against the benchmarks, debunk the correlation memo, set aside the $5.2B figure, and treat the competitor sample cautiously. Y uses the evidence slightly more fully. It gives the 17% versus 5% CAGR. It notes pilot month-on-month growth slowing from about 17% to about 9%, where X says only 'still climbing'. It runs volume sensitivities at 90% and 80%, the 38% ACoS extreme with peak $7.5M and margin 8.7%, and an exact 26.9% break-even under the higher duty; X approximates this as 'about 1.5 points' lower. It also stress-tests B across four cases and computes the 3.1× halo B would need to pay back. X has good unique items: 32 units per door to break even, 39% of category growth captured, and a note that the survey base is narrower than Table 8's. X's 'demand is proven' is a mild overclaim. Y's 'payback is likely on the planning inputs' and its 2032 extrapolation are slightly soft, though both are flagged.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CEO hypothesis as the key expects: keep the Amazon-first, retail-later sequence, add conditions, and move the awareness trigger from 15% to 20% because the 10–20% band's median of 3.5 sits below the 4.0 delisting bar. X adds test doors and a 4.0 sell-through check, and keeps the $10M trigger while noting it signals scale, not shelf readiness. Y goes a little further. It qualifies the $10M trigger with ACoS at or below 28% ('sales bought with heavy advertising do not prove the brand'). It adds a repeat gate and a self-funding retail-economics gate. It also replaces the fixed 2029 date with a gate decision at end-2028, noting that A's $2.4M headroom cannot absorb a national launch. Both make payback conditional on ACoS and reset the ambition.

overall.reasons: The two documents are substantively very close: same recommendation, same correct model outputs, same handling of the reasoning traps, and both meet all four defensibility criteria. Y would serve the board somewhat better. Its one-page test card, the quantified Japan trade-off, the stated accepted risk, the $4M envelope and the actionable ACoS guardrails give the decision maker clearer levers, and its retail gates follow through on the fixed-cost problem. It also adds sensitivities on volume, on break-even under the tariff, and on the halo B would need. X is rigorous and error-free, with a useful scorecard and a clear break-even derivation. But it is longer, sets its ACoS threshold at break-even with no buffer, and weighs Japan and the later retail economics less explicitly.
